chapters.title: Treaties at the edge of a new nation
chapters.lede: The new United States claimed the sole right to buy Native land and began making treaties to get it.
chapters.narrative: After the Revolutionary War, the United States wanted land and peace on a long frontier, and it turned first to treaties. At Fort Stanwix in 1784, the National Park Service says the United States took hostages from the Six Nations until prisoners of war were returned, and that signers may have been coerced. The Six Nations ceded interests in land west and north of an older boundary line. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 said the utmost good faith would be observed toward the Indians and that their lands and property would never be taken without their consent, a promise later treaties and wars tested again and again. States acted too. New York made its own treaties with the Oneida in 1785 and 1788, and the 1790 Non-Intercourse Act barred the sale of Indian lands to individuals or states without federal approval. That law set a rule that lasted for generations: only the federal government could acquire Native land. Native nations were not passive. They negotiated as sovereign powers and kept pressing their claims at the treaty table. The National Archives counts about 370 treaties made and approved by the Senate between 1789 and 1871, and this decade is when that long series began. On the map, the first transfers are modest and concentrated in the East.

chapters.title: Cessions in the Ohio country
chapters.lede: After Fallen Timbers, a string of treaties opened the Ohio Valley and drew a line of resistance.
chapters.narrative: The Treaty of Greenville in 1795 followed General Anthony Wayne's victory at Fallen Timbers on August 20, 1794. The West Virginia Encyclopedia says the nations of the region ceded about two-thirds of present Ohio. It became a model: military pressure first, then a treaty that put the cession on paper. Governor William Henry Harrison then negotiated a series of land treaties in Indiana territory, and the Treaty of Fort Wayne in 1809 was among the largest. The National Library of Medicine's Native Voices timeline records that Tecumseh questioned whether the leaders who signed had the authority to sell the land, and that after Congress ratified the treaty he warned Americans not to settle on it and organized people to resist incursions. The argument that no single nation could sell what many shared became central to the confederacy that Tecumseh and his brother led, and the conflict continued into the War of 1812. On the map, this period shows transfers moving from the Ohio River northward toward the Great Lakes. In the records they appear as treaties, but each one sits on a contested question: who had the right to sign for the land? Resistance was not only armed. It was also a claim about law and about the limits of any one nation's authority to give land away.

chapters.title: A doctrine and a policy take shape
chapters.lede: The Supreme Court wrote the right to buy Native land into law while states pressed to remove nations.
chapters.narrative: In Johnson v. M'Intosh (1823), Chief Justice Marshall wrote that discovery gave the government an exclusive right to extinguish the Indian title of occupancy, by purchase or by conquest. The same opinion described Native people as the rightful occupants of the soil, with a legal as well as just claim to retain possession. The ruling treated Native nations as holders of a right to occupy and treated the United States as the only lawful buyer. In 1824 the War Department created an Office of Indian Affairs. Meanwhile, pressure from states grew. The National Park Service writes that Georgia residents resented Cherokee success in holding onto their ancestral homelands, and that after gold was found on Cherokee land, efforts to dislodge the Cherokee intensified. Treaties in the Old Southwest and the Great Lakes continued to carve nations' lands into smaller pieces. By the end of this period, federal officials and state governments were openly discussing moving whole nations west of the Mississippi River. That plan would become law in 1830. The map in these years shows many smaller cessions across the South and the Great Lakes, each recorded in a treaty, and each one a step toward a policy that made removal, not purchase, the main tool.

chapters.title: Removal
chapters.lede: Congress authorized trading Native homelands in the East for land west of the Mississippi, and armies enforced it.
chapters.narrative: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 let the President set aside land west of the Mississippi for tribes that might choose to exchange the lands where they then lived. The National Park Service says it targeted the Five Southeastern nations in particular. The Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830) came first. EBSCO reports that the Mississippi legislature had voted to extend state jurisdiction over Choctaw lands, and that Choctaw leaders felt pressured and believed American power irresistible. The Choctaw ceded the remaining ten million acres of their land in Mississippi. The Seminole treaty of Payne's Landing (1832) was disputed; the Seminole Nation Museum notes that some Army officers said the chiefs had been wheedled and bullied into signing, and the Second Seminole War followed. The Cherokee Nation fought removal in court. In Worcester v. Georgia (1832) the Supreme Court described the Cherokee nation as a distinct community on its own territory where Georgia's laws had no force, but the ruling did not stop removal. The Treaty of New Echota (1835) was signed by a small group, and John Ross and the Cherokee Nation protested that it was not the act of the Nation. It was ratified anyway. In 1838 soldiers rounded people up into stockades and marched them west; NCpedia estimates about 4,000 of 15,000 died.

chapters.title: After removal, the frontier moves west
chapters.lede: Removed nations rebuilt in Indian Territory while the United States began looking past the Mississippi.
chapters.narrative: The removals of the 1830s did not end the pressure; they moved it. Removed nations had to rebuild homes and communities in Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma, after marches that the National Park Service describes as forced westward migration. The Second Seminole War ended in 1842. The Seminole Nation Museum calls it the longest and most costly of all the wars of removal fought by the United States, and says roughly 3,000 Seminoles had been removed to Indian Territory by its end. Many Seminoles resisted until the end, and the museum notes the war cost the government an estimated fifteen million dollars. In the Great Lakes and the Upper Mississippi, treaties kept moving land, and in New York the state continued its dealings with the Oneida, Onondaga and Cayuga that the National Park Service says opened land for settlers and speculators. By the late 1840s the United States was reaching across the continent, and the idea of a permanent Indian frontier was collapsing. Emigrant traffic began to cross the Plains. The Plains nations, whose lands lay along those trails, would soon be asked to sign treaties of their own. The map for this period is quieter in the East and about to change in the West.

chapters.title: Reservations and war on the Plains
chapters.lede: Treaties promised boundaries, and then the Army, miners and settlers crossed them.
chapters.narrative: As settlers and railroads pushed west, the United States turned to treaties that defined territories and then to smaller reservations. In the Treaty of Fort Laramie (1851), Plains nations recognized the right of the United States to build roads and military posts, and the treaty stated that they did not abandon rights or claims to other lands. In the Pacific Northwest, Isaac Stevens negotiated treaties such as Medicine Creek (1854), which paid $32,500 and secured the right of taking fish at usual and accustomed grounds; HistoryLink says not all those named actually signed. In Minnesota, the Minnesota Historical Society says the Dakota faced starvation in August 1862 when some factions attacked settlements. Thirty-eight Dakota men were hanged at Mankato on December 26, 1862, and the Dakota were forcibly removed from the state. On November 29, 1864, the National Park Service says, Colonel John Chivington led an unprovoked surprise attack on a peaceful camp at Sand Creek and killed more than 230 Cheyenne and Arapaho. The Navajo were forced to Fort Sumner on the Long Walk. On the map, these years show the first large cessions in the West and the reservations that came out of them. The record also shows how a treaty promise can turn into violence within a decade.

chapters.title: The treaties of 1868
chapters.lede: The last great wave of treaties set boundaries that nations still point to, and that are still argued over.
chapters.narrative: The 1868 treaties came after war. At Fort Laramie, the United States promised to close the Bozeman Trail and the forts along it. The treaty set apart a reservation for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the nations named in it. Article 12 said no cession of reservation land would be valid unless signed by at least three-fourths of all adult male Indians occupying or interested in it. That clause matters because the Black Hills were later taken by act of Congress. The Navajo treaty was signed at Fort Sumner on June 1, 1868. According to the National Archives, the Navajo were offered a choice between relocating to Oklahoma and returning home to their ancestral lands, and they walked home. The Navajo Nation Museum displayed the original treaty in 2018. The House Report on the Long Walk records that more than 3,000 Navajo people died from starvation and malnutrition during the captivity. These years are the high point of treaty-making as a way to recognize a land base. They are also close to the last. Congress was about to end the practice, and the new fights would be over whether the United States would honor what it had signed. The map shows reservation boundaries, many of which nations still point to as proof of promises made.

chapters.title: After the end of treaty-making
chapters.lede: Congress stopped making treaties with Native nations and changed land arrangements by statute.
chapters.narrative: On March 3, 1871, a rider to an appropriations act declared that no Indian nation or tribe within the territory of the United States would be acknowledged as an independent nation with whom the United States may contract by treaty. It did not undo old treaties: it said no obligation of any treaty lawfully made and ratified before March 3, 1871 was to be invalidated. The National Archives notes it ended the Senate's role in ratifying treaties. From then on, land moved by agreements, by executive orders that created or shrank reservations, and by acts of Congress. The Black Hills are the clearest example. After a war and an offer to buy that the Sioux refused, Congress took the Black Hills by act in 1877. In 1980, in United States v. Sioux Nation, the Supreme Court held that the 1877 Act effected a taking of tribal property and implied an obligation to pay just compensation. As former special trustee Ross Swimmer put it in a 2011 PBS report, they did not want the money; they wanted the Black Hills. The money was set aside but, as of that report, had not been collected. The map shows reservations shrinking by act and agreement rather than by treaty. Nations adapted by sending delegations, going to court, and holding their ground for generations.

chapters.title: Allotment and assimilation
chapters.lede: Federal law broke up shared reservations into individual parcels and opened the leftover land to settlers.
chapters.narrative: The General Allotment Act of 1887, the Dawes Act, authorized the President to allot reservation lands in severalty to individual Indians. Each allotment was held in trust for twenty-five years, and land left over could be sold to settlers. In 1889 the Sioux Act divided the Great Sioux Reservation into six reservations and, the North Dakota State Museum says, opened about 9 million acres of former reservation land to non-Native settlement. On December 29, 1890, soldiers killed Lakota people at Wounded Knee; History.com says almost 150 Native Americans were killed and some historians put the number at twice as high. Allotment was paired with boarding schools meant to assimilate children. The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 made all non-citizen Indians born in the United States citizens. The 1928 Meriam Report condemned the allotment policy. HistoryLink's account of the Puyallup shows how, in one case, virtually all allotted reservation land was taken out of tribal members' possession. The figure often cited for total loss across the allotment era is about 90 million acres, but it comes from secondary sources and we have not checked it against a primary count. Nations kept their governments, their claims and their communities, and many are still working to consolidate land that was divided.

chapters.title: Reorganization and termination
chapters.lede: Congress ended allotment, then tried to end the federal relationship with tribes, and dams flooded reservation land.
chapters.narrative: The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 provided that no land of any Indian reservation could be allotted in severalty. DocsTeach says it brought an immediate end to the nearly 50-year policy of allotment. The Act let the Interior Secretary acquire land for the purpose of providing lands for Indians, held in trust, and gave tribes the choice to vote on whether to organize under it. In 1946 Congress created the Indian Claims Commission. The National Archives says it could award money for lands lost but was not empowered to grant or restore land to tribes. The mood then turned. House Concurrent Resolution 108 in 1953 aimed to end federal supervision of tribes at the earliest possible time. The National Archives says Congress initiated 60 separate termination proceedings between 1953 and 1970 and that over three million acres of tribal lands were relinquished. In the same years, Missouri River dams flooded reservation land: a 1999 Senate report says 104,492 acres of Cheyenne River tribal land were inundated by the Oahe project. The effects reach into the present. In December 2025 Congress recognized the Lumbee Tribe, whose recognition had been limited by a 1956 Act, and its chairman said a relic of the Indian Termination Era had been erased. The map shows land leaving trust and tribal status in these years.

chapters.title: Self-determination and the first returns
chapters.lede: Protest, court rulings and new laws turned federal policy toward tribal control and a few land returns.
chapters.narrative: Native activism broke through in 1969, when Indians of All Tribes occupied Alcatraz Island; the National Park Service calls it the first intertribal protest action to focus the nation's attention. In July 1970 President Nixon told Congress that forced termination was wrong and that self-determination could be encouraged without the threat of termination. In December 1970 Congress returned 48,000 acres to Taos Pueblo. In 1971 the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, the Congressional Research Service reports, gave Alaska Natives approximately 45 million acres and a payment of about $962.5 million. The Menominee Tribe was restored to federal recognition in 1973. In United States v. Washington (1974), Judge Boldt held that Washington State had disregarded solemn promises made to the tribes in the 1850s. In 1980 the Supreme Court found that the Black Hills had been taken without just compensation. In 1990 the Puyallup Land Claims Settlement returned roughly 900 acres to the Tribe while the Tribe relinquished 20,000 acres, a mixed result that shows how returns can come with costs. These precedents are still in use. In 2021 Interior placed the National Bison Range, approximately 18,800 acres, into trust for the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes. On the map, trust land begins to grow again.

chapters.title: Apology, repair, and land coming back
chapters.lede: The federal government has apologized, returned some lands and recognized more nations, and the work continues.
chapters.narrative: On September 8, 2000, Assistant Secretary Kevin Gover formally apologized for the historical conduct of the Bureau of Indian Affairs, saying these wrongs must be acknowledged if healing is to begin. The Supreme Court's 2020 decision in McGirt v. Oklahoma asked whether the land the treaties promised remains an Indian reservation, and held that the Creek reservation had not been disestablished by Congress. That ruling put a removal-era treaty back at the center of law. In 2021 Interior transferred about 18,800 acres of the National Bison Range into trust for the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, and said the 1908 act that created the refuge reduced the Salish and Kootenai peoples' homeland by thousands of acres. In 2024 President Biden apologized for the federal boarding school policy, calling it one of the most horrific chapters in American history. In December 2025 the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina was recognized by Congress and describes itself as the 575th tribe. Some claims remain open. In a 2011 PBS report, the Sioux nations' leaders said the money awarded for the Black Hills had not been collected and that they wanted the land. This map shows the cessions the United States recorded. It cannot show what nations remember, hold and plan, and it should be read with that in mind.

sources.quote: The instrument in question is not the act of our Nation; we are not parties to its covenants;

moments.title: Cherokee removal
moments.text: Soldiers rounded up Cherokee families into internment camps and stockades and marched them west to Indian Territory. NCpedia estimates that about 4,000 of the roughly 15,000 who began the trek died. The Cherokee Nation was marched across several states in a forced removal.

sources.title: Trail of Tears, NCpedia
sources.quote: place them in various internment camps and stockades

sources.title: Trail of Tears, NCpedia
sources.quote: Of the approximately 15,000 who began the trek, an estimated 4,000 perished.

moments.title: First Fort Laramie treaty
moments.text: On the northern Plains, nations agreed to let the United States build roads and military posts, and the treaty named the territory of each nation. It also said the nations did not abandon rights or claims to other lands. Pressure on those territories grew with emigrant traffic.

sources.title: Treaty of Fort Laramie with Sioux, etc., 1851, Kappler, OSU Tribal Treaties Database
sources.quote: recognize the right of the United States Government to establish roads, military and other posts.

sources.title: Treaty of Fort Laramie with Sioux, etc., 1851, Kappler, OSU Tribal Treaties Database
sources.quote: the aforesaid Indian nations do not hereby abandon or prejudice any rights or claims they may have to other lands.

moments.title: Medicine Creek treaty in Puget Sound
moments.text: In Governor Stevens's first Washington treaty, Puget Sound nations ceded land for $32,500 over several years and kept the right to fish at usual and accustomed places. HistoryLink says not all those named actually signed. The fishing clause is the basis of treaty fishing rights today.

sources.title: Treaty of Medicine Creek, 1854, HistoryLink
sources.quote: pay to the said tribes and bands the sum of thirty-two thousand five hundred dollars

sources.title: Treaty of Medicine Creek, 1854, HistoryLink
sources.quote: the overwhelming historical evidence indicates that not all those named actually signed.

moments.title: U.S.-Dakota War and the removal after it
moments.text: After a summer of starvation, fighting broke out in Minnesota. On December 26, 38 Dakota men were hanged at Mankato, the largest mass execution in U.S. history, according to the Minnesota Historical Society. The Dakota were then forcibly removed from the state to Dakota Territory and what is now Nebraska.

sources.title: Background, U.S.-Dakota War of 1862, Minnesota Historical Society
sources.quote: In August 1862, with the Dakota facing starvation, some tribal factions attacked white settlements

sources.title: Background, U.S.-Dakota War of 1862, Minnesota Historical Society
sources.quote: On Dec. 26, 1862, 38 Dakota were hanged in Mankato in the largest mass execution in U.S. history.

moments.title: Sand Creek
moments.text: On November 29, soldiers led by Colonel John Chivington attacked a Cheyenne and Arapaho camp in Colorado. The National Park Service calls it an unprovoked surprise attack on a peaceful camp and says more than 230 people were killed. Today the site is a National Historic Site.

sources.title: Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site, National Park Service
sources.quote: killed more than 230 Cheyenne and Arapaho over the course of seven hours

sources.title: Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site, National Park Service
sources.quote: led an unprovoked surprise attack on a peaceful camp

moments.title: The Navajo return home
moments.text: After four years of captivity at Bosque Redondo, the Navajo signed a treaty at Fort Sumner. The National Archives says they were offered a choice between Oklahoma and their ancestral lands, and chose to return home. A House report records that more than 3,000 Navajo people died during the captivity.

sources.title: The Navajo Treaty Travels to the Navajo Nation, National Archives Prologue
sources.quote: returning home to Navajo ancestral lands

sources.title: House Report 107-222 (Long Walk National Historic Trail study), govinfo
sources.quote: More than 3,000 Navajo people died due to starvation, malnutrition

moments.title: Second Fort Laramie treaty
moments.text: After a war over the Bozeman Trail, the United States promised to close the road and the forts along it. The treaty set apart a reservation for the absolute and undisturbed use of the nations named, and required three-fourths of adult male signatures for any cession of that land.

sources.title: Treaties of Fort Laramie, North Dakota Studies
sources.quote: The government promised to close the Bozeman trail and the forts along the trail.

sources.title: Treaty with the Sioux, 1868 (Fort Laramie), Kappler, OSU Tribal Treaties Database
sources.quote: unless executed and signed by at least three-fourths of all the adult male Indians, occupying or interested in the same

moments.title: Congress ends treaty-making
moments.text: A rider to an appropriations act declared that no Indian nation or tribe would be acknowledged as an independent power with whom the United States may contract by treaty. Treaties already made stayed in force. The National Archives counts about 370 treaties approved by the Senate since 1789.

sources.title: 25 U.S.C. 71, Cornell LII
sources.quote: No Indian nation or tribe within the territory of the United States shall be acknowledged

sources.title: 25 U.S.C. 71, Cornell LII
sources.quote: but no obligation of any treaty lawfully made and ratified with any such Indian nation or tribe prior to March 3, 1871

moments.title: The Black Hills taken by statute
moments.text: Congress took the Black Hills by act in 1877, and the 1868 treaty had required the signatures of three-fourths of adult male Indians for any cession. In 1980 the Supreme Court held that the 1877 Act effected a taking of tribal property that required just compensation.

sources.title: United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, 448 U.S. 371 (1980), Cornell LII
sources.quote: Rather, the 1877 Act effected a taking of tribal property

sources.title: Treaty with the Sioux, 1868 (Fort Laramie), Kappler, OSU Tribal Treaties Database
sources.quote: unless executed and signed by at least three-fourths of all the adult male Indians, occupying or interested in the same

moments.title: General Allotment Act
moments.text: The Dawes Act authorized the President to allot reservation lands to individual Indians, to be held in trust for twenty-five years. Land left over could be disposed of to settlers. Over the decades that followed, much of the tribal land base passed out of Native hands.

sources.title: Dawes Act (1887), National Archives
sources.quote: to allot the lands in said reservation in severalty to any Indian located thereon

sources.title: Dawes Act (1887), National Archives
sources.quote: disposed of by the United States to actual and bona fide settlers only

moments.title: The Great Sioux Reservation divided
moments.text: The Sioux Act divided the Great Sioux Reservation into six reservations and opened about 9 million acres of former reservation land for non-Native settlement, according to the North Dakota State Museum. It is one of the clearest examples of a reservation being reduced by statute rather than treaty.

sources.title: The Sioux Act of 1889 and Its Modern Implications, North Dakota State Museum
sources.quote: divided the Great Sioux Reservation into six reservations

sources.title: The Sioux Act of 1889 and Its Modern Implications, North Dakota State Museum
sources.quote: opened about 9 million acres of former reservation land for non-Native settlement

moments.title: Wounded Knee
moments.text: On December 29, U.S. troops killed Lakota people at Wounded Knee Creek on the Pine Ridge reservation. History.com says almost 150 Native Americans were killed, nearly half of them women and children, and that some historians put the number at twice as high.

sources.title: Wounded Knee massacre, History.com
sources.quote: almost 150 Native Americans were killed

sources.title: Wounded Knee massacre, History.com
sources.quote: some historians put this number at twice as high

moments.title: Citizenship Act
moments.text: Congress declared all non-citizen Indians born within the territorial limits of the United States to be citizens. The Act created a federal status for individuals. It did not itself change the land held by tribes, which had already been reduced by decades of allotment and cession.

sources.title: Indian Citizenship Act (1924), Teaching Legal History, UNL
sources.quote: all non-citizen Indians born within the territorial limits of the United States

moments.title: The Meriam Report
moments.text: A major survey for the Interior Department condemned the allotment policy that had begun with the 1887 Act. Its findings helped turn opinion against allotment, which Congress ended within a few years, but land already lost did not come back to tribes.

sources.title: Meriam Report, EBSCO Research Starters
sources.quote: The report condemned the allotment policy that had been instituted with the passage of the General Allotment Act of 1887.

moments.title: Indian Reorganization Act
moments.text: Congress ended allotment and let the Interior Secretary acquire land for Indians, to be held in trust. Tribes could vote on whether to organize under the Act. It stopped the further loss of reservation land to allotment, though it did not return land already sold.

sources.title: Indian Reorganization Act, 1934 (statute text)
sources.quote: no land of any Indian reservation... shall be allotted in severalty to any Indian

sources.title: Indian Reorganization Act, DocsTeach, National Archives
sources.quote: gave tribes the choice to vote whether or not they wished to politically organize under the Wheeler-Howard Act.

moments.title: Indian Claims Commission created
moments.text: Congress created a commission to hear tribal claims over lost land. It could award money based on the value of land at the time of taking but could not restore land, so even successful claims ended in payment rather than return.

sources.title: Indian Claims Commission, National Archives
sources.quote: The ICC was established as an independent federal agency on August 13, 1946.

sources.title: Indian Claims Commission, National Archives
sources.quote: not empowered to grant or restore land to tribes

moments.title: Termination policy begins
moments.text: House Concurrent Resolution 108 aimed to end federal supervision of tribes at the earliest possible time. The National Archives counts 60 termination proceedings between 1953 and 1970, with over three million acres of tribal land relinquished. The policy was formally repudiated in 1970.

sources.title: Termination, National Archives
sources.quote: at the earliest possible time

sources.title: Termination, National Archives
sources.quote: over three million acres of tribal lands were relinquished as a result.

moments.title: Alcatraz is occupied
moments.text: Indians of All Tribes occupied Alcatraz Island from late 1969 into June 1971. The National Park Service calls it the first intertribal protest action to focus the nation's attention on the situation of Native peoples, and a turning point for American Indian activism across the country.

sources.title: Alcatraz Occupation, National Park Service
sources.quote: From November, 1969 to June, 1971, a group called Indians of All Tribes, Inc., occupied Alcatraz Island.

sources.title: Alcatraz Occupation, National Park Service
sources.quote: the first intertribal protest action to focus the nation's attention

moments.title: Nixon ends termination
moments.text: In a message to Congress, President Nixon called forced termination wrong and said self-determination should be encouraged without the threat of termination. The National Archives says his administration repudiated termination in 1970, marking the formal turn in federal policy. The message did not itself return land.

sources.title: Special Message on Indian Affairs (1970), Teaching American History
sources.quote: This policy of forced termination is wrong, in my judgment, for a number of reasons.

sources.title: Termination, National Archives
sources.quote: the Nixon administration repudiated termination in 1970 and shifted federal Indian policy toward self-determination.

moments.title: Blue Lake returned to Taos Pueblo
moments.text: Congress returned 48,000 acres taken in 1906 to Taos Pueblo. Taos Pueblo's own history page quotes the bill's statement that Congress now returns that land to whom it belongs. It was a rare large return of land by act of Congress.

sources.title: Blue Lake, Taos Pueblo
sources.quote: in 1906 an injustice was done in which land involved in this bill, 48,000 acres, was taken

sources.title: Blue Lake, Taos Pueblo
sources.quote: The Congress of the United States now returns that land to whom it belongs

moments.title: Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act
moments.text: Congress settled Alaska Native land claims with approximately 45 million acres and about $962.5 million, according to the Congressional Research Service. It was signed by President Nixon on December 18, 1971. We do not summarize Alaska Native views of the settlement here.

sources.title: Alaska Native Lands and the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (CRS R46997)
sources.quote: On December 18, 1971, President Nixon signed into law the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act

sources.title: Alaska Native Lands and the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (CRS R46997)
sources.quote: Alaska Natives received approximately 45 million acres

moments.title: The Menominee are restored
moments.text: Congress reversed the termination of the Menominee Tribe of Wisconsin and restored federal recognition. The Tribe's own history page describes the goal of restoration as reversing termination and regaining federally recognized status. It showed that a termination could be reversed by Congress, though only after years of organizing by the Menominee.

sources.title: Termination and Restoration, Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin
sources.quote: The goal of Restoration was to reverse termination and regain the Menominee's status as a federally recognized tribe.

sources.title: Termination and Restoration, Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin
sources.quote: The goal of Termination was to end Indian tribes' status as sovereign nations.

moments.title: Boldt decision upholds treaty fishing
moments.text: Judge George Boldt held that Washington State had disregarded solemn promises made to the tribes in the 1850s, and found the tribes entitled to up to half the catch. The Washington Secretary of State's history notes the ruling gave tribes standing to sit down with other governments as equals.

sources.title: The Boldt Decision, Washington Secretary of State Legacy Project
sources.quote: the State of Washington had disregarded solemn promises made to the tribes in the 1850s.

sources.title: The Boldt Decision, Washington Secretary of State Legacy Project
sources.quote: gave the tribes the standing—the power—to sit down at the table with other governments as equals.

moments.title: Sioux Nation ruling on the Black Hills
moments.text: The Supreme Court held that the 1877 Act took tribal property and that the United States owed just compensation to the Sioux Nation, with interest. The Sioux nations have not accepted the money; leaders have said they want the Black Hills, not payment.

sources.title: United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, 448 U.S. 371 (1980), Cornell LII
sources.quote: Rather, the 1877 Act effected a taking of tribal property

sources.title: United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, 448 U.S. 371 (1980), Cornell LII
sources.quote: That taking implied an obligation on the part of the Government to make just compensation to the Sioux Nation

moments.title: Puyallup Land Claims Settlement
moments.text: The Puyallup Tribe settled long-running land claims in Washington. HistoryLink says virtually all allotted reservation land had been taken out of tribal members' possession. The Tribe received roughly 900 acres and agreed to relinquish 20,000 acres, a trade that shows how returns can come with costs.

sources.title: Puyallup Land Claims Settlement (1990), HistoryLink
sources.quote: virtually all of the Puyallup Tribal members' allotted reservation lands were taken out of their possession

sources.title: Puyallup Land Claims Settlement (1990), HistoryLink
sources.quote: the Puyallup Tribe was to relinquish 20,000 acres of land and clear title to all land within Washington

moments.title: Apology from the Bureau of Indian Affairs
moments.text: On the agency's 175th anniversary, Assistant Secretary Kevin Gover formally apologized to Indian people for the historical conduct of the Bureau of Indian Affairs, saying that these wrongs must be acknowledged if healing is to begin. It was an apology by the agency, not by Congress.

sources.title: Gover Apologizes for BIA's Misdeeds, Bureau of Indian Affairs
sources.quote: I extend this formal apology to Indian people for the historical conduct of this agency.

sources.title: Gover Apologizes for BIA's Misdeeds, Bureau of Indian Affairs
sources.quote: These wrongs must be acknowledged if the healing is to begin.

moments.title: McGirt v. Oklahoma
moments.text: The Supreme Court asked whether the land promised by treaties to the Creek Nation remains a reservation, and held that Congress had not disestablished it. The case turned on what Congress had and had not done to a reservation created by removal-era treaties.

sources.title: McGirt v. Oklahoma, 591 U.S. ___ (2020), slip opinion, supremecourt.gov
sources.quote: Today we are asked whether the land these treaties promised remains an Indian reservation

moments.title: National Bison Range returned
moments.text: Interior moved about 18,800 acres of the National Bison Range into trust for the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes. Interior acknowledged that the 1908 act creating the refuge reduced the Salish and Kootenai peoples' homeland by thousands of acres. Congress approved the transfer by statute.

sources.title: Interior Transfers National Bison Range Lands in Trust for the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, U.S. Department of the Interior
sources.quote: approximately 18,800.22 acres

sources.title: Interior Transfers National Bison Range Lands in Trust for the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, U.S. Department of the Interior
sources.quote: this act reduced the Salish and Kootenai peoples' homeland by thousands of acres.

moments.title: Presidential apology for boarding schools
moments.text: President Biden formally apologized for the federal Indian boarding school policy and, as reported, called it one of the most horrific chapters in American history. The apology followed an Interior Department investigation of the boarding school system, which news reports say aimed to assimilate children and take tribal land.

sources.title: Biden first U.S. president to apologize for Indigenous boarding school abuses (news report)
sources.quote: one of the most horrific chapters in American history

moments.title: Lumbee recognition
moments.text: Congress recognized the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina. The Tribe's chairman said the injustice of the 1956 Act had been corrected, and the Tribe describes itself as the 575th federally recognized tribe. It is a late repair of a termination-era limit.

sources.title: Lumbee Tribe fully and rightfully recognized, Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina
sources.quote: The injustice of the 1956 Act has been corrected, a relic of the Indian Termination Era has been erased

sources.title: Lumbee Tribe fully and rightfully recognized, Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina
sources.quote: the Lumbee Tribe of N.C. is fully Federally Recognized as the 575th Tribe in the nation.
